idea.body:
I was thinking on an AI cooking app that would help the user to find recipes that he may like and guide him on the cooking.

For people who never know what to eat and want to try new food out.

The user choices over time and feedback over food tasted would make the algorithm more accurate and provide better options.

finding.title: Taste feedback may confuse preference with cooking success
finding.detail: A disliked meal could mean the recipe was a poor match or that cooking it went badly. Treating both as the same signal might make recommendations less accurate.

evidence.quote: feedback over food tasted would make the algorithm more accurate

question.text: After cooking, could feedback separately capture whether the user liked the dish and whether it turned out as intended?
question.why: This distinction would help the app learn taste without penalizing recipes for execution problems.

idea.body:
I was thinking on an AI cooking app that would help the user to find recipes that he may like and guide him on the cooking.

For people who never know what to eat and want to try new food out.

The user choices over time and feedback over food tasted would make the algorithm more accurate and provide better options.

For a new user, ask for three foods they like and ingredients they have, then suggest three recipes. They pick one and read one cooking step at a time. No voice guidance in the first version. We can test with a paper walkthrough before choosing technology.

finding.title: Choices may not reveal taste
finding.detail: A skipped recipe could reflect missing ingredients or effort rather than dislike. Treating every choice as preference data might narrow suggestions and work against trying new foods.

question.why: This determines whether recommendations learn food preferences separately from situational constraints.

dispositions.question: How should the app choose recipes before it has any feedback?

finding.title: Guidance may need to support recovery, not just instructions
finding.detail: Because users are trying unfamiliar food, they may encounter uncertain doneness, timing mistakes, or unexpected textures. The cooking experience could feel more helpful if it includes moments to check progress and adapt rather than only presenting sequential recipe steps.

evidence.quote: For people who never know what to eat and want to try new food out.

question.text: During cooking, should the first version mainly provide paced steps, ask users for progress checks, or help recover when something goes wrong?
question.why: Choosing one primary guidance behavior would clarify the experience you want to explore without requiring the whole cooking assistant to be designed.

evidence.quote: I want to explore how the cooking guidance feels.
